qt: to the Commission Lynn Boylan (The Left), Kathleen Funchion (The Left) Subject:

In its surveillance map of Lyme disease cases, the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) found fewer than 2 000 cases of Lyme disease in 20241. The map is based on testing corresponding to a document by ESGBOR, the European Society of Clinical Microbiology and Infectious Diseases (ESCMID) Study Group for Tick-Borne Diseases2. The leading institutions in ESGBOR are in Germany, Sweden, France and the Netherlands. ESGBOR members dominate the writing of guidelines for Lyme disease in these four Member States. The national patient groups in these countries do not endorse the resulting documents. ESGBOR promotes lumbar puncture as a testing method, which is much more invasive for the patient and more expensive than a blood draw. The burden and the risks for the patient are often downplayed. European Parliament petition 0986/2023, submitted by patient group EuroLyme, proposes a Lyme blood test comparison project with newer and evolved blood tests3. ESGBOR and by extension the ECDC’s mapping ignore these blood tests, despite the fact that EU regulations make the counting of all Lyme disease cases mandatory4. In light of this situation, how will the Commission ensure that data on Lyme disease reported to the ECDC accurately covers all diagnosed cases?

at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (20.10.2026) Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2018/945 included Lyme neuroborreliosis (LNB)1, rather than Lyme borreliosis as a whole, as one of the communicable diseases and related special health issues to be covered by the EU epidemiological surveillance network and established a specific case definition2. The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) data referred to in the question therefore concerns reported cases meeting this case definition and should not be interpreted as a count of all diagnosed Lyme borreliosis cases in the EU. The case definition was developed following ECDC scientific advice and consultation with Member State experts3. In particular, the diagnosis of LNB – which is the most severe manifestation of Lyme borreliosis – requires assessment of neurological symptoms and pleocytosis cerebrospinal fluid and/or intrathecal Borrelia-specific antibodies4; blood testing alone does not establish LNB according to the referenced clinical criteria. The Commission supports Member States in strengthening laboratory diagnosis of Lyme borreliosis through the EU Reference Laboratory for Public Health on High-Risk, Emerging and Zoonotic Bacterial Pathogens (EURL-PH-HEZB) 5, which covers Lyme borreliosis. The EURL-PH-HEZB provides reference diagnostics and test protocols, reference materials, external quality assessments, scientific advice, technical assistance and training. In 2026, the EURL-PH-HEZB is providing training on Lyme borreliosis laboratory diagnosis and in 2027 will organise an external quality assessment for national reference laboratories. These activities aim to strengthen knowledge and laboratory capacity on diagnostic procedures used for Lyme borreliosis.
